$comment: How raw open data becomes a live transit engine. This is a data pipeline, not a request path - draw it as a conveyor.

meta.title: Transit Data Pipeline - open data to live engine

image_prompt: Draw a data pipeline diagram, left to right, flat modern style, 16:9, like a conveyor belt of transformations. Start with two hexagon source shapes stacked vertically: 'Edmonton ETS GTFS - gtfs.zip, 22 MB, 7 agencies' and 'Geofabrik Alberta OSM - 350 MB'. The OSM one flows into a funnel-shaped box labelled 'clip_osm.py - cut to the bounding box of the feed's own stops' with a small map inset showing a large province shape and a small highlighted rectangle around Edmonton, and an output label '38 MB'. Both streams then converge into a big box 'OpenTripPlanner graph builder (Java 25, -Xmx6G)' with a stopwatch icon reading '37 seconds'. Output: a cylinder 'graph.obj - 96 MB, 291k vertices, 845k edges, 6,573 stops, 623 patterns'. That cylinder flows into 'gzip and publish as the rolling GitHub release transit-graph', then via a dashed arrow labelled 'scp' into a server icon 'EC2 /opt/rideiq/otp', then into an orange box 'rideiq-otp loads it (~60 s)'. Finally, three small feed icons on the far right labelled 'TripUpdates 45s', 'VehiclePositions 30s', 'Alerts 2min' point back into the orange OTP box with dashed arrows labelled 'GTFS-realtime, polled live'. Add a small warning badge near the GTFS source reading 'feed_end_date - past it OTP returns NOTHING, not stale times'.

style.look: flat, modern, professional, whiteboard-clean, generous whitespace
style.typography: sans-serif; keep all text horizontal; numbers in circles for ordered steps
rules: Green = pass / go. Red = blocked. Orange = automated trigger.
Every decision diamond must show both labelled exits.

stages.label: Fetch
stages.note: otp.py also downloads a private Temurin JDK if the system Java is older than 25 - OTP 2.9 will not start on 24

stages.label: Clip
stages.transform: cut the provincial extract down to a bounding box derived from the feed's own stop extent, plus a 0.05 deg margin
stages.why: handing OTP all of Alberta inflates build time and RAM for streets nobody in this app will ever walk on

stages.label: Build the graph
stages.output: graph.obj - 96 MB, 291k vertices, 845k edges, 6,573 stops, 623 patterns
stages.flags: FaresV2 enabled in otp-config.json - this is a BUILD-time flag, the fare rules are baked into graph.obj

stages.label: Publish
stages.output: gzipped onto the rolling GitHub release tagged 'transit-graph', with a graph-info.json recording the feed version and validity dates
stages.guard: the workflow FAILS if the freshly built feed expires within 14 days

stages.label: Ship
stages.transform: download the asset in the runner, scp it to EC2, unpack beside the live graph then swap atomically
stages.why: the host needs no GitHub credentials, and this keeps working if the repo ever goes private

stages.label: Load and serve
stages.runtime: about 60 seconds to load the graph into memory
stages.note: this is the ~1 minute window where /transit returns 503

realtime_feeds.gives: delays - every leg's clock time is delay-adjusted

annotations: The clip bounding box is derived from the feed, not hard-coded - if ETS adds a park-and-ride in Devon the box grows with it.

Trip updates only apply at about 61 percent. That is a feed property, not a misconfiguration: ETS identifies the rest with GTFS-realtime's newer modified_trip extension, which OTP 2.9 does not read for stop-time updates. In practice buses carry realtime and the LRT lines mostly do not.
Past feed_end_date OTP returns no itineraries at all rather than wrong ones - which is why the rebuild runs on a schedule and fails loudly when the feed is close to expiring.
